title: Chapter 22 — Why Democratic Nations Are Naturally Desirous Of Peace, And Democratic Armies Of War
paragraphs: The same interests, fears and passions that keep democratic nations from revolution also keep them from war. The love of military glory and the revolutionary spirit are weakened together, and by the same causes. Property owners, who love peace, grow ever more numerous. Personal wealth, which war consumes so quickly, keeps increasing. Customs have become milder and hearts gentler, with that inclination to pity which equality of conditions produces, and a coolness of understanding that leaves men relatively untouched by the violent, poetic excitement of arms. All these causes work together to extinguish the military spirit. I think it can be accepted as a general and constant rule that, among civilized nations, warlike passions become rarer and weaker the more equal social conditions are. Yet war is something every nation is exposed to, democratic nations like any other. However much they prefer peace, they must be prepared to repel an attack; in other words, they must have an army.

Fortune, which has granted the inhabitants of the United States so many special advantages, has set them in the middle of a wilderness, where they have, one might say, no neighbors. A few thousand soldiers meet their needs. But this is a peculiarity of America, not of democracy. Equality of conditions, together with the customs and institutions that follow from it, does not free a democratic people from the need for standing armies, and those armies always have a powerful effect on its fate. It is therefore especially important to ask what the natural tendencies are of the men who make up these armies.

Among aristocratic nations, especially those where birth is the only source of rank, the army has the same inequality as the nation. The officer is a noble and the soldier a serf; the first is naturally called to command and the second to obey. In aristocratic armies, then, the ordinary soldier’s ambition is held within very narrow limits. The officer’s ambition has no unlimited range either. An aristocratic body is not only one step on the nation’s ladder of ranks; it also holds a ladder of ranks within itself, and its members stand one above another in a fixed and unchanging order. So one man is born to command a regiment and another a company. Once they reach the farthest goal of their hopes, they stop of their own accord and are content with their lot. In aristocracies there is, besides, a strong reason why the officer’s desire for promotion is weak. Among aristocratic nations an officer, apart from his army rank, also holds a high rank in society, and in his eyes the first is almost always just an addition to the second. A nobleman who takes up the profession of arms follows it less out of ambition than out of a sense of the duties his birth imposes on him. He joins the army to find honorable occupation for the idle years of his youth, and to bring back to his home and his peers some honorable memories of military life. But his main aim is not to gain property, distinction or power through that profession, since he already holds these advantages by right and enjoys them without leaving home.

In democratic armies every soldier may become an officer. That makes the desire for promotion universal and extends the range of military ambition without measure. The officer, for his part, sees nothing that would naturally and necessarily stop him at one grade rather than another, and each grade matters enormously to him, because his standing in society almost always depends on his rank in the army. Among democratic nations an officer often has no property except his pay and no distinction except military honors. So whenever his duties change, his fortune changes, and he becomes, in a sense, a new man. What was merely an accessory to his position in aristocratic armies has become the main thing, the foundation of his whole condition. Under the old French monarchy officers were always addressed by their titles of nobility; now they are always addressed by their military rank. This small change in the forms of speech is enough to show that a great revolution has occurred in the structure of society and of the army. In democratic armies the desire for advancement is nearly universal. It is ardent, stubborn and unending; every other desire reinforces it, and only death puts it out. Yet it is easy to see that, of all the armies in the world, those where promotion must come slowest in peacetime are the armies of democratic countries. The number of commissions is naturally limited, while the number of competitors is almost unlimited, and the strict law of equality bears on everyone alike. No one can advance quickly, and many cannot advance at all. So the desire for advancement is stronger there, and the chances of advancement fewer, than anywhere else. Every ambitious spirit in a democratic army therefore longs ardently for war, because war creates vacancies and justifies breaking the rule of seniority, which is the one privilege natural to democracy.

We thus reach a curious result: of all armies, democratic armies are the most eager for war, and of all nations, democratic nations are the fondest of peace. What makes these facts more remarkable still is that the principle of equality produces both these opposite effects at the same time.

All the members of the community are alike, and they constantly harbor the wish, and see the possibility, of changing their condition and improving their well-being. This makes them fond of peace, which favors industry and lets each man carry his own small undertakings through to completion. This same equality, on the other hand, makes soldiers dream of battlefields. It raises the value of military honors in the eyes of those who follow the profession of arms, and it puts those honors within everyone’s reach. In both cases the heart’s restlessness is the same, the appetite for enjoyment is just as insatiable and the ambition to succeed just as great; only the means of satisfying it differ.

These opposite tendencies in the nation and the army expose democratic communities to great dangers. When the military spirit leaves a people, the profession of arms at once ceases to be honored, and military men drop to the lowest rank among public servants. They are little respected and no longer understood. The opposite of what happens in aristocratic ages then takes place: the men who enter the army are no longer of the highest rank but of the lowest. Military ambition is indulged only when no other kind is possible. This creates a circle of cause and effect that is hard to escape. The best part of the nation avoids the military profession because it is not honored, and the profession is not honored because the best part of the nation has stopped following it. It is then no surprise that democratic armies are often restless, bad-tempered and dissatisfied with their lot, although their material condition is usually much better and their discipline less strict than in other countries. The soldier feels he holds an inferior position. His wounded pride either stirs his appetite for hostilities, which would make his services necessary, or inclines him toward revolutions, in which he may hope to win by force of arms the political influence and personal importance that are now denied him. The makeup of democratic armies makes this last danger very much to be feared. In democratic communities almost every man has some property to protect, but democratic armies are generally led by men with none, most of whom have little to lose in civil strife. The bulk of the nation is naturally far more afraid of revolutions than in aristocratic ages, but the army’s leaders are far less afraid of them.

Moreover, as I have just observed, the wealthiest, best educated and ablest men in democratic nations seldom take up the military profession. So the army, taken as a whole, eventually forms a small nation of its own, where minds are less broadened and habits coarser than in the nation at large. Now this small uncivilized nation holds the weapons and alone knows how to use them. Indeed, the peaceful temper of the community increases the danger a democratic people runs from the military and turbulent spirit of its army. Nothing is so dangerous as an army in the midst of an unwarlike nation. The whole community’s excessive love of quiet continually places its constitution at the mercy of the soldiery. It may therefore be said, speaking generally, that if democratic nations are naturally inclined to peace by their interests and tendencies, their armies constantly pull them toward war and revolution. Military revolutions, which are hardly ever to be feared in aristocracies, are always to be dreaded among democratic nations. These perils must be counted among the most formidable that threaten their future, and statesmen should give careful and constant attention to finding a remedy.

When a nation sees that it is troubled from within by its army’s restless ambition, the first idea that comes to mind is to give this awkward ambition something to aim at by going to war. I do not speak ill of war. War almost always broadens a people’s mind and raises its character. In some cases it is the only check on the excessive growth of certain tendencies that arise naturally from equality of conditions, and it must be regarded as a necessary cure for certain deep-rooted diseases to which democratic communities are prone. War has great advantages, but we must not flatter ourselves that it can reduce the danger I have just pointed out. It only suspends that peril, which comes back more fiercely when the war is over, because armies that have tasted military exploits are far more impatient with peace. War could be a remedy only for a people that always thirsted for military glory. I foresee that any military rulers who may rise in great democratic nations will find it easier to conquer with their armies than to make their armies live at peace after the conquest. There are two things a democratic people will always find very hard: to begin a war and to end one.

Again, if war has certain special advantages for democratic nations, it also exposes them to certain dangers that aristocracies need not fear to the same degree. I shall point out only two. War gratifies the army, but it hampers, and often infuriates, the countless multitude of men whose lesser passions need peace every day to be satisfied. So there is some risk that it will cause, in another form, the very disturbance it was meant to prevent. No long war can fail to endanger the freedom of a democratic country. This is not to say that after every victory one need fear that the victorious generals will seize supreme power by force, as Sylla and Caesar did; the danger is of a different kind. War does not always hand democratic communities over to military government, but it must always, and immeasurably, increase the powers of civil government. It must almost inevitably gather the direction of all men and the management of all things into the hands of the administration. If it does not lead to despotism by sudden violence, it prepares men for it more gently, through their habits. Anyone who wants to destroy the liberties of a democratic nation should know that war is the surest and shortest way to do it. This is the first axiom of the science.

One remedy that seems obvious, when the ambition of soldiers and officers becomes alarming, is to increase the number of commissions available by enlarging the army. This gives temporary relief but plunges the country into deeper trouble at some later time. Enlarging the army may have a lasting effect in an aristocratic community, because military ambition there is confined to one class of men and each individual’s ambition stops, so to speak, at a set limit, so that it may be possible to satisfy everyone who feels it. But enlarging the army gains nothing among a democratic people, because the number of aspirants rises in exactly the same proportion as the army itself. Those whose claims were met by the new commissions are immediately followed by a fresh multitude that no one could satisfy. Even those who were satisfied a moment ago soon begin to want further advancement. The same excitement reigns in the ranks of the army as among the civilian classes of democratic society, and what men want is not to reach a certain grade but to keep being promoted. These wants may not be very large, but they come back without end. So a democratic nation that enlarges its army only calms, for a time, the ambition of the military profession, which soon becomes even more formidable because more people feel it. I am of the opinion that a restless and turbulent spirit is an evil inherent in the very constitution of democratic armies and beyond hope of cure. The lawmakers of democracies must not expect to devise any military organization whose influence could calm and restrain the military profession. Their efforts would use up their strength before the goal was reached.

The remedy for the vices of the army is to be found not in the army itself but in the country. Democratic nations naturally fear disorder and despotism; the aim is to turn these natural instincts into well-considered, deliberate and lasting tastes. When men have at last learned to use freedom peacefully and profitably, and have felt its blessings; when they have developed a manly love of order and freely submitted themselves to discipline; then these same men, if they take up the profession of arms, carry these same habits and customs into it, without realizing it and almost against their will. The general spirit of the nation, infused into the spirit particular to the army, tempers the opinions and desires that military life produces, or suppresses them through the mighty force of public opinion. Teach the citizens to be educated, orderly, firm and free, and the soldiers will be disciplined and obedient. Any law that, in suppressing the turbulent spirit of the army, tended to weaken the spirit of freedom in the nation and to cast a shadow over the idea of law and right, would defeat its own purpose. It would do far more to help than to hinder the establishment of military tyranny.

After all, and despite every precaution, a large army in the midst of a democratic people will always be a source of great danger. The most effective way to reduce that danger would be to reduce the army, but that is a remedy not every nation has the power to use.
